audit_scope.description: Trust model analysis for Ethereum Execution Layer components covering transaction processing, state management, fee calculation, genesis initialization, and wallet provider discovery mechanisms

components.name: Transaction Processing System
components.description: Handles transaction type identification, validation, and routing per EIP-7808

components.name: State Management System
components.description: Manages Modified Merkle Patricia Trie operations for state storage (Cancun fork)

components.name: Gas and Fee Calculation System
components.description: Performs memory alignment, exponential calculations for fee markets, and numeric utilities

components.name: Genesis Initialization System
components.description: Handles genesis block creation, configuration loading, and initial state population

components.name: Browser Wallet Provider System
components.description: Manages wallet discovery and provider announcement via EIP-6963

trusted_external_entities.name: Transaction Submitter (User/Sequencer)
trusted_external_entities.rationale: External users and L2 sequencers submit transactions to the node. These are untrusted inputs that must be fully validated for type identification, format compliance, and namespace authority per EIP-7808 and EIP-2718.

trusted_external_entities.name: Layer 2 Rollup System
trusted_external_entities.rationale: L2 rollup systems define RIP transaction types in the 0x40-0x7f range. While L2s have their own governance, from the L1 perspective they are untrusted and transactions must be validated against namespace boundaries to prevent cross-layer attacks.

trusted_external_entities.name: Genesis Configuration File
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: Genesis initialization (file system read from assets/ directory)
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Genesis configuration file contains critical chain parameters and initial account allocations. Although typically bundled with client software, a compromised file could pre-allocate funds to attacker addresses or set malicious parameters. Must be validated for hex format correctness, address validity, and parameter sanity.

trusted_external_entities.name: Wallet Browser Extension
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Wallet extensions inject code into the browser page context and announce themselves via EIP-6963 events. Extensions are untrusted as they can be malicious, impersonate legitimate wallets, or attempt prototype pollution attacks. DApps must freeze provider details and render SVG icons safely via tags only.

trusted_external_entities.name: Malicious Browser Extension
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Explicitly malicious extensions attempting wallet impersonation, code injection, or prototype pollution. Represents the adversarial model for EIP-6963. Must be mitigated through Object.freeze(), duplicate UUID detection, and safe SVG rendering practices.

trusted_external_entities.name: End User
trusted_external_entities.rationale: End users select wallet providers from discovered announcements. Users are untrusted in the sense that they may be socially engineered into selecting malicious providers that impersonate legitimate wallets. DApps must provide clear visual cues and validate provider info to help users make informed choices.

boundary_edges.target_component_interface: Transaction Processing System (RPC eth_sendRawTransaction or P2P transaction gossip)
boundary_edges.security_assumption: All incoming transactions are untrusted and must be validated for: (1) EIP-2718 typed transaction envelope format compliance, (2) transaction type namespace authority (EIP vs RIP range per EIP-7808), (3) signature validity, (4) nonce correctness, (5) sufficient gas and fee payment. Invalid transactions are rejected before state transition.

boundary_edges.target_component_interface: Transaction Type Routing System (namespace boundary checking)
boundary_edges.security_assumption: L2 rollups are untrusted to properly allocate RIP transaction types. L1 nodes must validate that transaction types in the 0x40-0x7f range are processed according to L2 RIP rules and not mistakenly treated as L1 EIP types. Namespace isolation prevents cross-layer transaction processing confusion.

boundary_edges.target_component_interface: Genesis Initialization System (file read and parsing)
boundary_edges.security_assumption: Genesis configuration file is untrusted input that must be validated for: (1) valid JSON structure, (2) correct hexadecimal format for addresses and values (0x prefix handling), (3) valid 20-byte addresses via hex_to_address(), (4) parameter sanity checks. Malformed or malicious genesis files must cause initialization failure rather than creating a compromised chain state.

boundary_edges.target_component_interface: Browser DApp Wallet Discovery System (EIP-6963 event handling)
boundary_edges.security_assumption: Wallet extensions are untrusted code executing in the browser page context. DApps must: (1) freeze provider detail objects with Object.freeze() to prevent modification, (2) validate UUIDv4 format and detect duplicates to identify impersonation, (3) validate RDNS format per RFC-1034, (4) validate icon data URIs per RFC-2397, (5) render SVG icons only via tags to prevent script execution, (6) never inline SVG content. Provider details are hints only, not security guarantees.

boundary_edges.target_component_interface: Browser DApp Wallet Discovery System (EIP-6963 event handling)
boundary_edges.security_assumption: Malicious extensions attempt wallet impersonation, prototype pollution, and code injection. Mitigations include: (1) Object.freeze() on all provider detail objects to block prototype pollution, (2) duplicate UUID detection to identify impersonation attempts, (3) strict SVG rendering via tags only to prevent XSS, (4) visual warnings for suspicious providers. Users are the ultimate defense and must be provided with clear comparison cues (name, icon, RDNS).

Users are untrusted to correctly identify legitimate wallet providers. DApps must present provider information clearly with validated fields (name, icon, RDNS) and warn about suspicious indicators (duplicate UUIDs). The interface must not mislead users or obscure security-relevant information. User selection is final trust decision point.

notes: All truly external entities have been identified and have corresponding boundary edges defined.
Four entities (EXT-GAS-CALCULATOR, EXT-FEE-MARKET, EXT-CRYPTO-OP, EXT-VALIDATOR) were misclassified as external but are actually internal execution layer components.
The analysis covers five distinct subsystems: transaction processing (EIP-7808), state management (Cancun trie), numeric utilities, genesis initialization, and wallet provider discovery (EIP-6963).
EIP-6963 introduces a unique trust boundary in the browser environment where multiple untrusted extensions compete for user selection.
Genesis file is treated as untrusted despite being bundled with client software to account for supply chain attack scenarios.
All boundary edges specify concrete validation requirements and security assumptions that must hold for system security.
